utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. As far as I understand, there are no preliminaries. Therefore, could -- Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There is one preliminary matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just briefly. Your Honour, I forgot to mention last week with respect to 92 bis the following: In keeping with the Chamber's guidance, the Prosecution is endeavouring to use statements and not rely on testimony. But there are a number of cases where there is no suitable statement and the Prosecution is concerned that the process of going out, sending a team out, to take the statement, to bring it back to translate it and -- and should the Chamber grant our 92 bis application to then send another team out from the Registry to swear it or have the witness swear to the statement, would not only be very costly but could delay our ability to complete the 92 bis process, so we are asking the Chamber to consider giving us an opportunity to file a test case, as it were, of five witnesses where we believe Mr. McCloskey has been looking at it very carefully and we believe we can make a selection of prior testimony that would no more than 30 to 50 pages and we believe would read essentially like a statement. So we're a seeking permission from the Chamber to file an application of five witnesses for which we do not have amalgamated statement or a statement that's suitable, and that way the way Chamber would have before it an example of what we think would be suitable evidence to be tendered 98 bis and would be able to make a more informed decision about whether this is a suitable way to proceed. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any response to this, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know, we do not like any curving of the rules, and at this moment provisionally we would object. But if you give us more time we will respond either orally or in a written way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if my recollection serves me well, we have expressed our strong preference for statements, and I think that in the guidance, but please, correct me when I'm wrong, there is also something about good cause being shown if it is burdensome for the witnesses. Now whether you have to go twice or whether you can already have the statement translated at a distance and taken at a station right away is a practical matter in which I'll not -- on which I'll not comment at this moment. But I think that if you make an application which meets what the Chamber requires to make an exception to what it expects as a rule, of course, it's difficult to say in advance whether or not we would agree with it. Much may depend on the reasons you're giving.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to say that the category of witnesses that I'm referring to, I don't think that we would be able to represent that it would be so distressful -- the process of another statement that we would meet that retirement of the Chamber. It is simply that it would be so time exhuming and costly we submit that there is a better way to proceed and we'd like an opportunity to demonstration that to the Chamber in a limited filing of five witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will wait and see what you present, Mr. Groome, and we'll then decide on whether or not it's -- it follows your suggestion that this is the better way to proceed. Certainly, the amount of pages played a role in expressing our preference for statements rather than for testimony -- transcript of testimony I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We will prepare that filing, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll use the time to deal with a late notification of Rule 92 quater motion. On the 23rd of July of this year, the Prosecution filed a motion for admission of evidence of three witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 quater. For some reason, this filing was not distributed to the Chamber until last Friday. There was no Defence response to the motion so the Chamber allows for the possibility that this filing also never reached the Defence and, in light of this, the Chamber hereby sets the response deadline for this filing to the 15th of October, 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness, Mr. Merdzanic, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, you'll first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli. Ms. D'Ascoli is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to your right. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you, first of all, state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: My name is Idriz Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And now what is your ethnicity, sir?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, do you remember providing a statement to the ICTY on 27 and 28 of August 2000?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can the Court Officer please display 65 ter 28115 on our screens, which is the witness statement. And, for the record, we have uploaded a hand numbered version the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, once the document is on the screen before you, can you please look at the very first page of the English statement and, in particular, the signature at the bottom of the page and can you indicate whether you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read and review this statement in preparation of your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. As regards my testimony today, I was given the statement to read it before it began.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I ask the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 28444. Your Honours, this was the table of correction and clarification. It has been now assigned a 65 ter number, which is the one that I just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, once again, when you can see the document on the screen, can you please have a look at it and can you confirm that you had an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the document I received so that I can review it before the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And does this document accurately set out the corrections and clarifications that you wanted to make to your statement?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is correct. After I had reviewed my statement, I noticed in several places that there were things that needed to be corrected. We had a conversation about correcting it, and these are the actual corrections that were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And taking into account these changes, these corrections and clarifications, are you satisfied that the statement is a accurate record of your evidence of what happened and what you experienced, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if you were asked today the same questions, would you give approximately the -- well, would you give the same answers, in substance, and provide the same information?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They would be as reflected in the corrections.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And now that you have taken the solemn declaration that you affirm -- that you provided the information in the statement and in the correction and clarifications, in accordance with the truth, and you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of this statement, as corrected?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can affirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 28115 and 28444, pursuant to Rule 92 ter as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 28115.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 269 - Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at you, no objections - is admitted into evidence. The next one, the corrections and clarification, 28444.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P270 is admitted into evidence. It seems that someone is constantly touching his microphone, which produces noise in our earphones. Yes, it's gone. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are also -- there were 27 associated exhibits to Mr. Merdzanic's statement. But upon review we decided to not to tender them all but we will only tender eight. These are five diagrams drawn by the witness and explained in the witness statement and also three of the photos taken by the witness in Trnopolje camp. If I -- maybe I can enumerate them individually if that can assist so that you also have the correspondence between the 65 ter number and the -- the identification that is used in the statement, because of course the 65 ter number is not in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I take them one by one. The first one is 65 ter 18278.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, which is referred to as IM-1 in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18278 becomes Exhibit P271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 65 ter 18421, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think 421 is the one that we just read, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we had 278. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I'm sorry, that was my mistake. Therefore, just for the record, 18278 is IM-4 in the witness statement. The following one you mentioned, 18421 is IM-1 in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And receives, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Next one, 18422, diagram IM-5, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, diagram IM-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Receives, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P273.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 65 ter 18427, a photograph of the interrogation room, IM-B attached to the 2000 ICTY statement receives.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P274, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, when I make a mistake you'll correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 65 ter 18429, a photograph referred to as IM-D in the statement receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P275, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. 18435, a photograph, taken by the witness, IM-I in the statement receives.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 18565, diagram IM-2 receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. 18567, diagram referred to as IM-3 in the statement receives number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With the Chamber's permission I will now briefly summarise Mr. Merdzanic's evidence for the public and the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Idriz Merdzanic is a doctor who worked as physician in the health centres in Kozarac and Trnopolje in 1992. The witness testifies about the attack on Kozarac on 24 May 1992 and the shelling of the town which continued for two days. He provides evidence about his efforts to treat people for injuries received from shelling and infantry weapons and how a number of people died as a result of injuries received during the attack. And this relates to Indictment Schedule A 6.1. He testifies about the surrender of the Muslim population on 26 May 1992 and about seeing Serb soldiers looting houses. He witnessed the bussing of many citizens primarily women, children and elderly to Trnopolje camp, which is in Indictment Schedule C 15.4. This witness testifies about the conditions at Trnopolje camp where he was detained from 26 May until the 30 of September, 1992. As a doctor in Trnopolje camp, the witness provides unique information about the conditions in the camp and the camp personnel. He describes the inhumane conditions of detainees in the camp, including disease, lack of adequate food or hygiene, beatings, rapes and killings occurring in the camp, and this refers to Indictment Schedule B 13.5. The witness also testifies about an increase in the prisoner population of Trnopolje camp due to the attacks and the systematic expulsion of the Muslim population from the villages of Prijedor municipality. And this concludes the summary of evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, now that I have summarised your written evidence, I'm going to ask you some questions to expand or clarify upon this evidence. First of all, sir, in 1992, you were employed as a physician under the Prijedor health centre and you worked in many satellite health clinics in the Prijedor municipality; for example, the clinic in Kozarac. Do you know anything? Did you ever hear of the dismissals of non-Serb medical staff from Prijedor and Kozarac health centres in the first half of 1992 after the takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I had occasion to hear about it after the camp was disbanded, since my wife was also a physician working at the health centre in Prijedor. I learned that the manager of health centre, Mr. Bereta [phoen], summoned all of the medical employees in early June to come to the centre where he singled out Muslims and Croats, telling them that they are no longer welcome and that they shouldn't come to work any longer. That's what I learned from my wife.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Merdzanic, I will move to the events in Trnopolje camp where you were detained from 26 May to 30 September. Sir, you say that at the time of your arrival there, you had no idea you had arrived at a prisoner camp. And, for the record, this is paragraph 26 of your statement. Now my question is: When did you become aware of that? When did you form the idea that Trnopolje was a prisoner camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The next day, or two days later, we learned that we can no longer leave Trnopolje, although no explanation was given as to why. When Major Kuruzovic arrived we handed over a list of personnel in the outpatient clinic and he told us that none of us was allowed to leave. We also learned and saw, actually, that guard posts were set up around Trnopolje and that no one could leave or enter on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So you say that no explanation was given as to why. So I take it that you were never told -- or, actually, let me put it in this way. Were you ever told at that moment or later on during the months between May and September were you ever told why you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. No one ever offered an official explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And of which ethnicity were the other people also in the camp, detained at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, of course, because of your role there in -- in this house clinic there, Trnopolje, you spoke to many people and did any of them told you that they were given a reason, they were told why they were detained in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, there was no explanation that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, it would be helpful if we could have the document on the screen, his statement, P269, with the respective paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sure. I was discussing paragraph 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, based on your -- what you experienced and what you saw in Trnopolje, the people you treated, the people you talked to in the camp, I mean, in your opinion why -- what do you think was the purpose of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the purpose of the camp at Trnopolje was to implement the process of ethnic cleansing in Prijedor municipality, which was effected by the Serbs moving out entire village populations, village by village. First, they would separate women and children from able-bodied men, and they would take the women and children to Trnopolje. Perhaps there were about 10 per cent of men in the overall number who arrived. From Trnopolje, convoys were organised to have the people transported. At first, it was by railroad in cattle wagons that were loaded and the people moved outside the Serb territory, as they referred to it. The mopping up, as they called it, of villages was always done in the same way. I know that because everyone arriving there was telling basically the same story. The able-bodied men were imprisoned in other facilities or camps or killed on sight or taken in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doctor I have two follow-up questions from what you just told us. First, I want to start from the very last part of your question [sic]. You say: "The mopping up, as they called it, of villages was always done in the same way." What do you mean when you say "as they called it"? What do you mean by "they"?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: By "they," I was referring to the Serbs, mainly the military. They would go into the village, round it up, expel the whole population from their houses, and then divided them into groups. Thereafter, they would be expelled from the village. Those who were able bodied were mainly taken to Omarska. A small portion of the population came to us. And then, after that, the villages were either looted or if they didn't have any need for it, they would set houses on fire, including churches and mosques. Probably the intention behind that was to prevent people from ever coming back.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, my second question in relation to what you told us was -- I was going to ask you an explanation of what you say in paragraph 38 of your statement, namely, that the number of women and children and elderly held in Trnopolje was much higher than the number of military-aged men. And, as you said today as well, that the military-aged men represented only the 10 per cent of the population. And I wanted to ask whether you had an explanation about that and whether you knew where the military-aged men were going but I understand from the answer you just gave us that the military-alleged were mainly taken to other camps, and you mentioned Omarska, in particular. Is that correct? Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Those who came to Trnopolje the majority of them remained there so with time the number of men in Trnopolje increased. They were still searching for some people on a daily basis and if they managed to locate them, they would beat them up or just take them away. As for the others who came from the villages, the able-bodied men, most of them were taken directly from the villages to Keraterm or Omarska, or perhaps some other place.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you also discuss in your statement how the guards would beat detainees. This is, for example, paragraphs 47 to 51, or 53 and 57. And also that rape and sexual assault took place in Trnopolje, perhaps 32 and 33, for the record. And you also comment upon the few women who came forward to say that they were actually raped or sexually sexual assaulted. This is at paragraph 63 and 66. Now, Dr. Merdzanic, as a doctor, what can you say about the physical and psychological impact that rapes and sexual violence had on these women considering that some of them came forward and talked to you about that? What can you tell us about the physical and psychological impact of these rapes on women?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I believe that the major psychological problem, in addition to the problem of their possibly becoming pregnant and bearing children to their rapers, there were other social problems in that these women didn't know how to explain that to their families or their husbands, what happened. And I think that the psychological effects are the worst of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doctor, I would now like to ask you a few questions about the camp authorities. In paragraph 35, you mention that Slobodan Kuruzovic was the camp commander, and you also say that Kuruzovic would take orders from higher officials. We find this in, for the record, paragraph 36. Doctor, can you tell us what led you to believe that he was receiving instructions from someone superior to him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that the basis for that understanding was that every time they first had to wait for an approval from higher level for any convoy. This approval came either from Prijedor municipality or Pale, but I cannot tell you exactly. Anyway, they waited for an approval for each and every convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you about the deputy commander of the Trnopolje, Slavko Puhalic, whom you mentioned in paragraph 35. Could you describe what he wore in terms of clothing or uniform in the camp.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He was dressed in military camouflage uniform of colour green.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In your statement you also name the guards who were most involved in the beatings. This is paragraph 52. My question is: Would the camp commander, Kuruzovic, have been aware of killings in the camps, beating and sexual assault, which the detainees were subjected by the camp guards, insofar as you know or insofar as you have seen?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that he did know, although he personally never beat anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: What about the deputy commander, Slavko Puhalic, would he have known about it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Slavko Puhalic certainly knew about it, because Slavko Puhalic was one of those who called people by name, such as the relatives of Gutic who was a student working with us in the clinic. After he had learnt that the two were there, he called two uniformed men in military uniforms from Prijedor and took them to a room where they beat them. And after that, they drove them away in a small vehicle. That indicates that Slavko Puhalic must have known about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And as far as you know, were these beatings or killings ever either investigated or -- was any action taken about them? In particular, did Kuruzovic do anything about these beatings or killings that were happening in the camp, for what you have seen?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. No investigation was ever conducted concerning the killings and the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And was any action ever taken by Kuruzovic directly in the camp to stop this?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Not with regard the people being taken away - the beatings and the killings - not that I know of. I don't know if he undertook any measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Dr. Merdzanic, now I would like to ask you a few questions about the visit of journalists to Trnopolje camp on the 4th of August, 1992, authorised by Karadzic. And you mention this at paragraph 70 to 72 of your statement. My question is: What did the camp guards or officers in the camp do when they knew of the arrival of journalists in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They first attempted to remove as many inmates from the camp as possible. For that purpose, they organised a convoy in which nearly all the women and the children left the camp. The first male convoy was organised, and the first such convoy that I photographed left Trnopolje and so they provided space in Trnopolje in order to be able to bring in the inmates from Keraterm and then from Omarska. Later on, we found out that they had completely closed down Keraterm and transferred the inmates from Keraterm to Trnopolje, and some of them were taken or actually one group of the people confined in a hangar were just shot dead one morning, and one group completely disappeared. They applied the same practice with Omarska. A group of inmates were sent to Manjaca, another group was kept in Omarska, but they were given beds and food to be shown to the journalists. And a third group, they hid in lorries and buses so that after Penny Marshall had left, they were brought to us at Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Let me clarify this bit by bit. You mention the arrival of people from Trnopolje -- sorry, from Keraterm and Omarska; for example, you mentioned that a group of detainees was transferred to Trnopolje from Keraterm, after the journalist visit on 4th of August. This is in paragraph 53 of your statement. So I guess you speak to them while you were in Trnopolje. You speak to these detainees coming from Keraterm; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had an opportunity to talk later. Initially we were not allowed to speak with them, but as soon as the journalists arrived, they were actually in Trnopolje camp in a part which was fenced in order to keep them separate from us. Later on, after Penny Marshall had left and the news about the camps was broken, they soon thereafter removed this wire fence, and people were able to move freely, and their relatives from Prijedor and other places were allowed to come in and bring food to the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And when you finally -- when you got the chance of speaking to these people that were transferred to Trnopolje from Keraterm, what did they say, if anything, about what happened in the hangars at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, they told us that they had been beaten down there regularly. They described this hangar, that one morning machine-guns were placed there, that the gates were open, and that some 200 people were shot dead inside the hangar. At the beginning, we were rather reluctant to believe that something like that could happen. But later on I met Enes Crljenkovic, a man who survived the shooting in the hangar, and after I had talked to him I became convinced that that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I see that the name of the survivor that you mention has not been captured in the transcript. Would you mind -- so his first name is Enes. Would you mind spelling the last name for the record, please. His family name?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Crljenkovic. It's C-r-l-j-e-n-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have the same questions also with regard to the detainees that were transferred from Omarska. You mentioned this in paragraph 71 of your statement. What did they tell you, if anything? What did they tell you about what happened in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, inspectors from Prijedor and Banja Luka as they referred them to, came on a regular basis to interrogate the inmates. They were beaten on a regular basis. And that there was a facility called the white house. Anyone who was taken to the white house never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doctor. Let's go back to the first visit by journalists when Penny Marshall and other international journalists came to the camp on 4 August 1992. You describe this in paragraph 72 to 73 of your statement. There, you say that when they came to the clinic, a Serb medical technician, missing an arm, Mica Kobas, was present. And you didn't dare say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show you a clip taken from the video filmed at Trnopolje camp during this first visit of Marshall and other journalists. This is it 65 ter 22591A, which is a clip of a little over a minute taken from a video by the ITN. The originator was Penny Marshall. The video was sized by the OTP from ITN in June 1996. Now for the record the frame we selected correspond to minutes 00:00:28 to 00:01:45 of the original video which bear the 65 ter number 22591 from which the clip has been created. I will now ask Ms. Stewart to play this video but before we play twice I would like first to show some frames so that I can ask some preliminary questions to -- to the witness. So I would ask Ms. Stewart to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- please stop at the very first images of the video. I think this would be second 4 so that I can ask the witness a preliminary question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you provided the booth with the transcripts or are there no words spoken?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We do have transcripts of the video which are uploaded in e-court, are then provided to the booth -- ah, okay, Ms. Stewart did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, in two languages?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, in two languages, B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we please stop here.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, can you describe what you see what is depicted in this frame?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is a waiting-room at the clinic. The man in the forefront, that's me. The person to the right in white coat is a Serb called Mica who was present there. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, can you please repeat the name of the Serb you just mentioned. The name wasn't captured in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: His name was Mica Kobas.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So this is the person you described in paragraph 70 to 73 of your statement, the Serb who was present in the clinic when the journalists arrived; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I now ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, I'm a little bit confused about the man in the forefront and the person to the right in a white coat. I see two persons with white clothing: One to the right of a person who is a little bit further down, and one to the left of him. Which one is you?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This -- the person -- Mica Kobas is the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness. I'm asking the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Oh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This person in the middle, facing forward, that's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can go back to 00:04. Mica Kobas is more visible. Yeah, exactly. This is the frame --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm that this is Mica Kobas who was missing an arm and is visible from the video?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is correct. He had only one arm. That's Mica Kobas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, in order to understand the testimony we have to put on the record what we saw a minute ago which was not at 4 seconds but 5 seconds, 40, approximately, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. At 5 seconds we saw Mica Kobas moving at the very front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at 5.4 and we later looked at 4.4.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: 4, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we now continue playing the video and stop at approximately 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We actually stopped at 18.7. And now I'll ask the witness to describe what -- the persons we see in the video.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The one in the foreground, that's me. Behind me is Gutic Vasif, a medical student. And the person sitting down is one of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now we can play the video one time for the interpreters and then a second time for the courtroom. From the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And now the video will be played a second time, and we will have the transcript from the booths. The translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Penny Marshall: Does he get any cases here of people who'd been beaten in other camps? "Merdzanic: Yes. "Penny Marshall: Many? "You have a lot of medicine or do you need more medicine? Need more medicine? "Merdzanic: Yes. "Penny Marshall: You are working very hard, hard work. "Merdzanic: Hard. I'm in the camp as the others. "Penny Marshall: Do you speak Russian or English? "Interpreter: Do you speak Russian or English? "Penny Marshall: Would you be happy to speak in another language? "Merdzanic: Just a little Russian. "Penny Marshall ... Conversation conditions in Russian.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doctor, I have only a couple of questions with regard to what we saw, as you described already what was depicted. During this interview with the journalists in your clinic, did you feel free to talk and describe the situation in the camp?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We were not allowed to speak freely because Mico Kobas was present there. We tried to give a signal to Penny Marshall that we wanted to remain alone with her, and I think that eventually she got the message, and she asked Mico Kobas to leave the room for a short while. At first, he refused to do that, and they entered into an altercation, after which he did leave the room for about a minute or two. And during that time, we managed to hand over the camera that we used beforehand to make a couple of photos. She wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sorry, you can complete your sentence and then I'll have a last question.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: She wanted to give us the camera back and keep only the film, but we were afraid that the Serbs would find the camera, so we gave her everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Doctor, my last question about this video. At some point after -- immediately after Penny Marshall ask you about the cases of beatings in the camp, we see -- you don't answer, and we see a strange expression on your face. How would you describe that expression that you had?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know myself how I would describe it exactly. This was our chance to hand over that camera. In a way, we tried to make her realise that we could not talk to her properly while Mica was present there, and that we wanted to talk to her on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see it's time for the break, after which I will only have one other clip to show to the witness, and that will conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it was indicated that you would need 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now at 50 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I think so -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... therefore, we'll take a break. But, first, could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I, meanwhile, put on the record that when I invited you, Ms. D'Ascoli, to correct any mistake I made, at that same moment I made a mistake. I had forgotten to rule on the admission of P274, which is hereby done. P274 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I forgot to ask for the admission into evidence as a public exhibit of 65 ter 22591A, the video that we just showed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection. Madam Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22591A becomes Exhibit P279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P279 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I will now ask you to have a look at another clip from a video. This is 65 ter 22471A, which is a clip of approximately a minute, taken from a video titled: Dzavid, part 2, which was brought to the Tribunal in January 2000 by Nasret Sivac [phoen], former journalist in Prijedor. For the record the frames we selected correspond to minute 00:37 to 00:38 of the original video which bear 65 ter number 22471. I will now ask Ms. Stewart to play 65 ter 22471, and before we do so, if we can stop at this very first image of the video so that I can ask the witness a preliminary question. Yeah, exactly. At the -- 00, the very beginning of the video. Dr. Merdzanic, do you recognise the man who is being interviewed here, the man on the left-hand side of the screen, with the white shirt?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is Dr. Stakic, who worked in Omarska and who was in the SDS. He held a post there. I cannot remember what it was exactly. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: This clip can now be played one time, first for the interpreters who have been provided with English and B/C/S transcripts, and then a second time for the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will now ask Ms. Stewart to play the video a second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: "[Voiceover]: We are talking to Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff. Mr. President, please describe to us the situation in the territory that is under your control. "Milomir Stakic: Well, I can tell you and the viewers that the whole territory of Prijedor municipality is under our control, which I can confirm following the liberation of Kozarac. The town, Serb settlements or neighbourhoods and smaller enclaves with Muslim population have been under our control since the takeover of power on 30th April, and now, after the fall of Kozarac, the entire municipality is under our control. In Kozarac itself, this operation of mopping up, as the military call it, is still under way because those who have stayed behind are the most extreme ones and professionals."

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Merdzanic, I want to -- I want to ask you to comment upon a couple of things that Dr. Stakic said in this interview. First of all, "The whole territory of Prijedor municipality is under our control which can I confirm following the liberation of Kozarac." Dr. Merdzanic, you have experienced the takeover of Kozarac and the situation in the Prijedor municipality. Can you confirm or not, on the basis of what you saw in the territory of Prijedor that the Prijedor municipality was under Serb control -- control, following the takeover of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That is correct. He himself said that the military unit took over Prijedor on the 30th of April. It was only Kozarac, and I think Hambarine and Carakova that were left. When these two locations fell, then Serbs had full control over the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Next, can you comment on the expression that Dr. Stakic used, "the liberation of Kozarac"?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, "liberation." If it weren't sad, it would be ludicrous. In Kozarac almost 100 per cent, or at any rate over 95 per cent of the population was Muslim. That's the way it had been always. Who did they liberate it from? They killed people, they expelled them from their homes, and then they claim to have liberated Kozarac. Liberated of whom and for whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, finally, can you comment upon -- about the last expressions that you used that I think has been here translated with "the mopping up of the territory as the military call it." Can you tell us what you intend -- what's your understanding of mopping up of the territory, as the military use the term?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They use that all the time when we were in Trnopolje, at the camp there. They kept saying that they were mopping up or cleansing, one village after the other. Although it's not logical now when they say that they had full control over Kozarac. Why would they do that in all the villages then? There was no fighting. There was no resistance. Why did they carry out this cleansing or mopping up or, rather, this expulsion of the Serbs -- or, rather, the non-Serbs from their homes. They were being killed too. They called that "ciscani [phoen]."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mopping up as a military term, cleansing as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And just to clarify the record you say carrying out the expulsion of the non-Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Merdzanic. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I tender 65 ter 22471A into evidence as public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22471A becomes Exhibit P280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And that concludes my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Lukic, you'll cross-examine the witness, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, doctor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's been a long time since we've seen each other, since Stakic. Doctor, the title speaks for itself, that you are more than we will educated. Nevertheless, I have to ask you about some kind of special education and training, whether you have that because of certain special legal aspects of this trial. Do you have any formal training or did you study social relations between or among separate social groups?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have no special training --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer because the interpreters did not catch it. You have no special training in what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no special training in terms of studying these social relations among ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you do not have any formal training in political science and that you never studied the causes of the war?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have not completed any kind much of political science school.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you study military strategy and artillery ballistics?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not study that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you study military command and control?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. Just like all others from the former Yugoslavia, I did my military service, so I roughly saw how this worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have not been trained as a lawyer; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have not been train as a lawyer, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not study demographics either?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, why not ask the witness whether he studied anything else, the medicine, and whether he has any experience as in when he did his military service. Then we have excluded. Because you can ask him whether he studied gastronomy -- or, I mean, let's try to keep it simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is in line with our objections we filed on 92 ter motion for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not saying it is irrelevant to know but why not as it in a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the future we can do that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You just ask: Did you study anything else than medicine and is your military experience, does it go beyond what you experienced when you were serving in the military. Then in one or two questions you have exactly the information which now takes two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not depriving you from the information. I'm just encouraging you to obtain it as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, actually we're going to abandon this area now and we are going to move on. In this case, it has been already been established that Muslims and Croats did not respond to military call-up. You added that people were hiding so that they could not be found by those who were enforcing the military call-up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Even some Serbs did not respond to the military call-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, so I'm pausing. People were hiding because they could have been prosecuted and convicted.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, those who did not respond to the call-up would lose their jobs or, for example, if they were policemen, if they did not sign an oath of loyalty to the Serbs and the Serb republic, they could no longer stay on in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1992 or 1991? What you said just now, in your answer.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to deal with the takeover in Prijedor. You yourself said that the Serbs bragged, saying that they had taken over without having fired a single bullet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Overnight a military unit arrived from Croatia and took over Prijedor overnight, as far as I know, without firing a single bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the takeover of Prijedor, did normal life continue in town?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Normal life did not continue in town. A curfew was imposed. Also, searches started, searches of houses. They were saying that they were looking for concealed weapons, and they started interrogating people. People were taken to the police station, interrogated, and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to focus my questions on the period from the 30th of April, that is to say, the date of takeover, until the 22nd of May when the conflict in Hambarine broke out. So I would like to ask you that we focus on these 20 or so days. Did people continue going to work except for those who held political office and who, through this change or coup were removed from these political positions?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At that time most people still went to work except for some who were hiding so as not to be send to the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that after the takeover this situation suited the Serbs, that they had an interest in not having anything changed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, as far as I know. Actually, could you tell me why the Serbs took over Prijedor in the first place? Democratic elections had taken place. If they were satisfied with that, why did they want a military takeover of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably my question was not very precise. I meant after the takeover were they satisfied with the situation? I mean, if we want to call it this mini coup d'etat.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You have to ask the Serbs about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. This situation, did it suit you, the Muslims, this Serb takeover in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At first I thought -- well, in principle, people were not satisfied with that but they did not do anything about it, for as long as the Serbs left them in peace. However, after the takeover, they were no longer left in peace. Searches started, and people were being taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the 22nd of May until the 30th of May, three attacks took place: In Hambarine, Kozarac, and Prijedor. Do you know what actually happened in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I heard that -- I mean, Hambarine is also a Muslim area and Serbs wished to enter Hambarine. The Territorial Defence had check-points there, or guards, and there was a conflict. And in that conflict, there were some fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that conflicts took place. Did you hear of any Muslims being wounded or killed in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not there, but I know one thing. It wasn't Muslims from Carakovo that attack the Prijedor. But it is the other way around, Serbs from Prijedor attacked Carakovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that, actually, fire had been opened on people who were in a passenger car at Hambarine check-point?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that. I wouldn't know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to move on to the ultimatum to Kozarac. Do you know that a military column was moving along the road from Banja Luka to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that the military column had been attacked and that the first driver in this military truck had been killed.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it. From you. Now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That means that you also did not hear that the column that was moving to Prijedor actually stopped in Jakupovici just before Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: How could it be stopped when Serbs held the entire road from Prijedor to Banja Luka? There were tanks there and check-points. They held the entire road under their control. Even the intersection at Kozarac. That's where there was a tank too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether you heard of the attack against the military column in Jakupovici on 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I've not heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So there was a ultimatum that was issued before this date. And before this date is it correct that in Kozarac people in uniform and people out of uniform carried weapons?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, most people who had weapons either had Territorial Defence uniforms or -- what was he called? Esad Cirkin. Civilians. There weren't very many civilians who carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Territorial Defence of Kozarac having three and a half thousand members?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on. Don't exaggerate. There weren't that many inhabitants in th first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the arming of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see the weapons being brought in? Were you present?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I have never even heard of weapons being brought into Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know what kind of weapons there were in Kozarac and how many?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I was at the infirmary and it's only once or a few times that I went to the outskirts of Kozarac where Cirkin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we have been mentioning Cirkin, you saw 15 persons in uniform around him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's where they were. And perhaps at the positions there were others, but I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They also had similar military uniforms, green military uniforms, and uniforms of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time did you know, or did you find out later, who Sead Cirkin's superior was?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I do not know about him having any kind of superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in his staff?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was on his staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly what the wording was of the ultimatum of the Serb authorities to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, an ultimatum was issued with the date of surrender, when they were supposed to surrender. I cannot tell you exactly what the ultimatum was. I was just a civilian there working at the infirmary. I just heard from other people what was going on. I was not organised from a political point of view, from a military point of view. I did not belong to the authorities in any way, so I would not have any insight as to how this exactly developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know then or do you know now who issued the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that one of the negotiators was Stojan Zupljanin. Now, as for who issued the ultimatum, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you learn that Zupljanin issued an order that it wasn't mandatory in -- for Prijedor and another municipality?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I am unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the conflict which preceded, you were tasked by Sead Cirkin to set up a plan for medical assistance for those who might get wounded.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It is completely incorrect. Sead Cirkin provided no instruction or order to me to set up an outpatient clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say you were in contact with him, and he told you to do things by yourself and to set up a health clinic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's not correct in the way you put it. He provided no instruction. There was about -- there were about ten civilians who gathered, and we decided to help civilians and people who might be injured. It had nothing to do with the TO or Sead Cirkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you wanted to assist the civilians and people who might become injured.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Anyone who needed assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Including soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even Serb soldiers. We even had a Serb soldier who was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I make no difference. A patient is a patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us move onto the issue of fighting in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have exhibit 65 ter 18273.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is still not on our screen, doctor. We will dwell on this topic briefly. It is a map. We see the title: Kozarac-Omarska Overview. So this is supposed to indicate the area of Kozarac and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you mark for us where that tank was which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Oh, the image is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do bear with us. Place a T where you think the tank was.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: At the intersection, approximately where the red dot is. That's where the tank was placed even before the attack and ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please use the pen again to mark Jakupovici for us, both Gornji and Donji Jakupovici.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't see them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It should be in the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, here. Jakupovici. Gornji Jakupovici. As for Donji, yes, this is where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not leave Kozarac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are done with the map. While you served your military term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you want to tender it, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Map 18273 as marked by the witness in court becomes Exhibit P281 Your Honours. Sorry, I apologise, it should receive D number. So it becomes Exhibit D55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D55 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, may I ask you what kind of a map this is. Is this, again, such a map with a not 90-degrees projection, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My understanding is this is more sketch. We received it from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I see that there's a scale of kilometres. Now scales indicating kilometres do not work on maps unless they are 90 degrees projected maps; because, otherwise, it distorts the distances, et cetera. I would urge the parties only to use maps which are free from such distortion. Mr. Groome, the Prosecution, I've noticed in many other cases is very good at providing maps which are of a bad quality because they are not the 90 degree projection, just from the top to the bottom but rather under a certain angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can investigate this particular map and see what its projection is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because distances, we get lost if we do not have the right projection. But for the purpose of this marking, I think it's no real problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor you said that you served your regular military term and you told us where. Let me ask you this: Were you in contact with any artillery units while serving in the army?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, not directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that shells fell and exploded incessantly. One could say that it was around-the-clock shelling for two days. These are paragraphs 12 through to 18 of your statement. Let me ask you this: Kozarac and its environs it is a densely populated area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You can see it on a map. It depends what standard you apply. By European standards it is not densely populated. Perhaps in Balkan terms it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many inhabitants were there in the area at the time in Kozarac and Kozarusa?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many wounded were there, due to the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can only say that as for those who managed to reach us because due to the shelling very few did, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you offer a figure? I counted 6 or 7 people. I don't know if I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was one dead there. There was one with a wound to the thorax; two children; two women. Well, a total of nine, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, you're better placed to know the figure. We'll accept that. At a certain point on the 25th of May, 1992, the shelling stopped; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can repeat: When the shelling began on the 24th, it went non-stop throughout the night until the next day. Then there was a short break of two to three hours. Perhaps there were talks going on, or something else. And then shelling resumed until the next day, when there was a surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have partially answered my next question. I wanted to ask you if you knew about the negotiations in the midst of fighting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I was not privy to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is obvious that the negotiation round on the 25th was unsuccessful since the shelling resumed.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I really can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to hear on Radio Prijedor what it was all about?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, the Serbs cut off all telephone lines and there was no -- there were no radio reports of any attacks. In any case, I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see civilians leaving Prijedor -- sorry, Kozarac for Prijedor, since they were called upon to leave Kozarac and come to Prijedor to take shelter because of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never heard about that. How was one to leave if there was shelling non-stop? Kozarac was being shelled where the houses and civilians were rather than any positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about it later, that many civilians, indeed, followed the instruction and took shelter in Prijedor with their families and relatives?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: People could not leave Kozarac because of the shelling. Only once Kozarac surrendered the civilians were supposed to leave. I don't know what the situation was in the outskirts though. I was in the hospital all the time, and I only have partial information. I don't know what was taking place further afield. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you learn later, or perhaps at the time, that wounded people kept arriving in the Prijedor hospital, both Serbs and Muslims, throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yourself that after the clash, the wounded were transferred to Prijedor to the hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I said that the wounded were the first to leave. There was this Lugar, who was Serb, and a boy. They were taken to Prijedor. The boy died later on. There was another wounded person in the chest, and a driver, but they were taken to Omarska, to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What are the names of the two people who were directly taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: One of them was the husband of Azra, the vet, the veterinarian. And for the other one --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was his last name Blazevic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think his last name was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you can recall. If not, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't. The other person was Sefik. I believe that was his first name. I can't recall the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us discuss the surrender of Kozarac now. You said that Nihad Bahonjic was singled out and killed when they reached you. He was your driver; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was not when they reached us at the outpatient clinic. We were taken from the outpatient clinic on foot to the centre of Kozarac. We waited there for a while -- for a while, and that's when he was singled out. When they were -- when we were picked up by a military jeep, we heard two shots being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if he participated in attacks on certain Serbs immediately preceding that period?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that while I was in Kozarac, during the attack, he was with us, throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why was he singled out? Was it a kind of revenge? What was your impression?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. They asked him for an ID. He did so. And that's when he was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Even after the surrender, some remained fighting. Some of the fighters withdrew to -- towards Mount Kozara?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the police force surrendered and they were all killed immediately after the surrender. Cirkin, with his men, set off across Mount Kozara. They were captured later on. So if we compare how many of them were captured, which was about a dozen with your figure, you mentioned 3.000. This is an illustration of how many people there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about a counter-attack on Kozarac in an attempt to seize it again by Muslim forces which were led by Kemal Alagic, aka Divljak?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. By that time I was in the camp in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to Trnopolje then, which is paragraph 26 and onwards in your statement. Which facilities or around which facilities were people situated, those people who were brought at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There was an outpatient clinic and the local commune building as well as the cultural hall. Some were there, while others were in the school. When there was no more room there, they were also placed in the construction material store. When that became full, people were forced to sleep outside on the grass, between the school and the hall, up as far as afield as the pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of Trnopolje, where these people were accommodated, there's a railroad track; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was this railway built?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. This was the railway that connected Banja Luka, Prijedor, and further on, towards Zagreb, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can agree that it was built tens of years before that.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that this was not something that was built prior to the event.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was there already, and they knew very well that it was very convenient to use cattle carriages to transport people further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if it was there already then it was built prior to the event, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That was my understanding. I just wanted to check. Because there is some statement from this witness telling something different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the guards in Trnopolje there were Muslims as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know that there were Muslims among the guards. I know that there were two men who once came from the front and were looking for their families in the camp, because whilst they were in -- on the front line, their families had been taken away and killed. But these two were not guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding, Mr. Lukic, when you said that -- there's some statement from this witness telling something different, that is not in evidence or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it comes out, I would be able to address this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we please have P277 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, will be so kind and mark the place where Penny Marshall was standing during her first visit.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Penny Marshall entered through this place, and that's the construction materials store, and this fence used to exist before. Now, there was a small passing or opening in the fence. She passed through it and reached this bigger fence. The Keraterm inmates were locked up here. A new fence was put up there. And the other one was repaired, and this is where the prisoners were kept. And she filmed them from this area, I think. But there are some shots from different angles as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, in order to understand the marking, I think, please follow me, the blue dot, lowest, is the place where she entered the -- what was the literal text. The material shed. The cross above that, slightly to the left, is where she filmed. Now, further up, there are two lines, to the left and to the right of the words "Serb Red Cross." That is where the witness said the new fence was made. And the cross immediately below the "Serb Red Cross," that is where the detainees were. Better is, next time, to invite the witness to mark with --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Change the mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to at least use letters or whatever, if you instruct him better. But I think it's now clearly on the record. Ms. D'Ascoli seems to agree as well. But marking usually is best done by using letters or by giving clear instructions. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I made three such sketches: There's one before the journalists arrived, there's one when the journalists arrived, and the one after they had left. And maybe the best way would to be use sketch number 2 where all the relevant positions of journalists are marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have now used this one. I leave it in the hands of Mr. Lukic whether he wants to use another one as well. But what you said is now reflected by your markings, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, P277, as now being marked by the witness will receive number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit D56, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D56 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. I'd like to add one thing. Within this fence were the prisoners from Keraterm; whereas, the rest of them were still in school. I wanted to say this in order to avoid any misunderstanding. And I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear and on the record by now.
