utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going ask you something in connection with this. Penny Marshall is filming the people who had been brought from Keraterm, or was she filming the people who were not brought from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, she was filming the prisoners brought from Keraterm and a smaller group of them arrived earlier from Omarska but the majority were from Keraterm; because most of people from Omarska arrived only towards the evening, after Penny Marshall had gone. They were also put inside the fence where this construction materials store is located; the place where she entered the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that this fence was built to confine the people from Keraterm immediately before the journalists arrived, and then the fence was removed after they left.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Once the world and Europe learned about the camp by television broadcast, they hastily removed the fence. So one segment of the fence was newly built, and there was an older fence that used to exist before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. They know that the journalists are coming, they put people inside the fence, and as soon as the journalists leave, they tear-down the fence; isn't that counter-productive?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no plan for journalists to come to Trnopolje. They were supposed to go to Omarska, but then they were sent from Omarska to Trnopolje, and, as far as I know, they were already passing through Trnopolje when journalists, by chance, saw some people. They removed the fence only after my photographs were published and after Penny Marshall basically provided proof of the existence of the camps. They were probably under the pressure from the public, and an instruction came from Karadzic or whoever for this fence to be removed, and they even allowed family visits from Prijedor, in order for the prisoners to get some food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you -- you asked for opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the witness happily enough did provide 90 per cent of his answer by giving facts. I think it's better to ask a witness of fact about facts, rather than to elicit opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm also looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness first be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the opportunity to remind the parties that they were instructed to file by the 26th of September their positions as to how much material should be uploaded into relation to D20, which is the report of the Netherlands institute for war documentation. I don't think that we have seen any filing not from Defence, nor from the Prosecution, or have we?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. Stojanovic have been discussing it. I believe they have come to an agreement. Perhaps he can illuminate us what that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we will hear from them then at a later stage. It's then true that we have not received any written submissions that were filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Lukic. There were no consultations in court anymore. That was the new regime. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fence that you said was built, the new one, can it be seen in the film made by Penny Marshall? You must have seen them.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it can be seen in Penny Marshall's film.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, the fence around the school is just an ordinary fence. How tall was it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, about 70 centimetres, up to 1 metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So one could easily jump over it.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At which point were people free to come and leave Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When you say "people," are you referring only to males, or are you referring to women and children as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to women, children and the elderly. When there they were allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The women and children were mainly transported elsewhere. When an announcement came that the journalists were going to visit the site, the women who had arrived from Omarska beforehand were sent off to Prijedor. After the journalists' visit and before the International Red Cross came and the fence was torn down due to the fact that it was known that there were camps, women used to come but mainly to visit and to bring food. There were some exceptions, though, that some of the women came to the camp of their own accord. They mostly came in an organised way, by buses, following the mopping up of their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some men left as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. A smaller portion of the male population managed to do that, if a Serb managed to put them on a convoy. And I said that was organised before the journalists arrived and before the others arrived. A convoy was set up before the International Red Cross registered the detainees. I'm talking about the convoy of detainees who were killed at Mount Vlasic. In that period, Major Kuruzovic who had received confirmation that there was place to accommodate them before being registered, they let them go. For example, my wife's father was also set free, but later on, in Prijedor, he and his wife and the wife's sister were killed in their house, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I gained the impression that your first question, which was at which point were people free to come and leave Trnopolje, the witness then asked what you understood by "people." And that there's some confusion as what "leaving" means in this respect. The witness apparently is talking - that's at least how I understand his testimony - about when people left Trnopolje; whereas, your initial question seemed to be to what extent people were free to leave and come back and go to their homes and then return to Trnopolje. Is that what you wanted to ask? Because that's not what the focus of the answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with this answer, Your Honour. Maybe when it is translated it sounds differently. But I think witness and I understood each other properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, it's also for the Chamber, of course, to understand what you apparently -- let me ask it clearly. You have told us about convoys leaving or women taken out before the journalists came. To what extent were those detained men, women, children, elderly - if there's any distinction, please make it - were able to leave Trnopolje, go home and then return, or even not return. Could you tell us something about the freedom of movement in and out Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, mostly -- I mean, well, when the journalists came, no one could enter or leave without receiving permission from the Serbs. Until that arrival, after cleansing the these village, they mainly brought in women and children. Only about 10 per cent were men. And then women and children were transported further on from Trnopolje to territories outside the Serb republic. When it was announced that the journalists would come, then men were released in this one convoy too. They were allowed to leave, as well as women, to create room for these others. After the journalists came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there because your answer again is apparently focussing on people taken to other places. My question is about, if, for example, a woman or small number of men were brought to Trnopolje, or came - some of them, you said, voluntarily to Trnopolje - were they free then to leave and go home again and then to return, or should they stay, apart from the convoys taking them out. But on an individual level, could they go home, for example, to look after their vegetable garden and then return with some food or -- and was that allowed to everyone? This is a very compound question. Apologies for that. Could you please tell us something about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is it a bit complicated, that's what I can say. Because in different stages there were different relations within the camp. At any rate, it was never possible for the civilians to decide themselves, Now I'll go to the camp, then I'll go home and then I'll come back again. They had to receive permission to do that. For example, at one point in time they even allowed male inmates to go not to their own homes but to houses around the camp that were empty to look for food because there wasn't enough food in the camp. There wasn't enough food so they allowed them to go in search of food. They also allowed them to bring in some wood-fueled furnaces but then nobody could do that without any kind of control. It's not that I could go home and then return whenever I wanted to. No, that did not happen. It was only after they allowed this, after the journalists and before the Red Cross, namely, that woman could come to the camp and visit the inmates that had been registered. Then after the International Red Cross, and after the journalists, they allowed these visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, even if people would leave if someone would manage to escape, could they move around or were there front lines around the entire area?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were only check-points. Now whether there were more conflicts going on. I don't know. I don't know if there were further conflicts. If somebody managed to escape then it was possible, well, I mean, like out of any prison anybody can try to escape and some succeed and -- but where do they go? Serbs were going from one house to another, checking everything. Houses had also been torched. I think that there was no point in trying to escape anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Didn't conflicts start in Bosnia-Herzegovina as soon as the camp was opened?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about conflicts in Prijedor. As far as you remember, Dr. Stakic himself said on TV that Serbs held under their control -- well, unless you're saying now that he was not saying the truth at that point in time on television that's a different matter. But the Serbs themselves were saying that Prijedor had been taken care of. That it was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Obviously this interview had been given before the 30th of May, because there's only a reference to Kozarac. So could -- so Dr. Stakic did not know what the situation was in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, he was president of the SDS, and he'd have to -- well, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the subject of Stakic, I saw that you said that he was a member of the SDS. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the date of the interview known in one way or the other? Because you're drawing conclusions. Obviously it has been given because there's only a reference -- if you know the dates then if the parties could agree on that, then we don't have to deduce by logic when the interview was taken. Anyway ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution can help.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm checking the MFI information for the video, Your Honours, but we don't have the date of the interview itself. We have the date of the -- when the video was seized and brought to the Tribunal, but there is no date of the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- and I remember there was no date on the video either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know that Dr. Stakic was a member of the Veljko Guberina Radical Party, not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now this is why I asked whether you had anywhere to go. You heard about the opening of the corridor towards Serbia on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I hadn't heard of the opening of the corridor towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You hadn't? All right.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I hadn't. But what would I be doing in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Towards Croatia there was fighting there. Towards Croatia and in Croatia. Then towards the part that was under the control of the TO BH, later on the army of the BH, there was also fighting. Could you leave at all crossing the confrontation line at any point, if this were not organised?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was not allowed to leave at all. Secondly, my opinion is that all of those who were fit for military service -- well, the Serbs left them there on purpose because they were afraid if they would let them go somewhere then they take up weapons - probably - and fight together with the BH army to return to their homes. That's why the Serbs decided to kill them and not to let them go. This is just my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to deal with facts and I'd like to talk about the conditions in Trnopolje itself. From paragraph 31 onwards, a few paragraphs. First question: When you came to Trnopolje, you were not searched or frisked; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's right. We were not. Only Azra Blazevic had a rucksack. No one else had anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All the time in Trnopolje, you had your personal documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I did not have my documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court 1D300. We need -- actually, in line 1 they asked you -- I'm going to read it in English so you can receive the proper interpretation: [In English] "Did you have your personal documents on you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Yes, I had my ID." [Interpretation] That's what you said under oath in the Stakic trial on the 11th of September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was your memory better, more fresh then than today?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you accept that you did have your personal documents on you throughout your stay in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can say that they did not take our documents away. I think that that is sufficient. I mean, I cannot recall the actual image now, having my ID there. Maybe I did have it; maybe I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it at that. Now I'm going to ask you about the registration of people in Trnopolje. Was that done from the very beginning or actually from when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Registration in Trnopolje? That was not carried out, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We received that information in independent television news LTD. On the 8th of March, 2000, you testified 02095901, 51 to 53, lines 51 to 53. This is what you said, that from the very outset registration was carried out in Trnopolje. Would you recall that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that we had to compile a list at the infirmary and hand it over to Kuruzovic. As for the others who were in camp, except for when they left, then they had to sign this. I don't know of any special registration, especially not all these women and children who spent only a night or two there and then were transported again. I do not remember this registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. As for the conditions in Trnopolje itself, is it correct that guards tried to help people?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I never claimed that all Serbs were bad. There were some people who want to the help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there other Serbs from the surrounding area who tried to help?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were other Serbs who tried to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, the locals, the people who lived around the area, Serbs included, you say brought food to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But, as I've said, these were just individuals. Even the Serb lady who was with us, Goga was her name, she was in Kozarac with us at the infirmary there, and she was taken to Trnopolje together with us. She wanted to stay on with us in Trnopolje, but they did not allow that, and they kicked her out. She's Serb too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Red Cross arrived in Trnopolje, the local Red Cross, on the 28th or 29th of March [as interpreted], 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly which day that was. I cannot guarantee that. At any rate, it was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did they have in order to help the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had anything available. I just know that they did not bring anything. Now, whether they had something available, and did not, or whether they did not have anything available, I mean, I cannot say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, doctor. Just a technical matter. Page 58 of LiveNote, line 22, it say "the 28th or 29th of March." And I think that my question referred to the 28th or 29th of May. And I believe that that is how the doctor understood it too. Let us move on. Do you know where this assistance for Trnopolje arrived, the assistance that did?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Which assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross take part in this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you should seek confirmation if it's your understanding that the witness understood something. Then you should seek confirmation rather than to -- to express what you believe is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, we have to go back to this 28th and 29th. I asked you when the Red Cross arrived, and you said towards the end -- or the beginning, or, rather, the beginning when it was established.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When Trnopolje was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's May, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It's either the end of May or the beginning of June. But it's just during those few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that members of the Red Cross from Prijedor asked the International Red Cross for help?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you communicate with members of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We did communicate with Pero Curguz and Dusko Ivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you suggest to them to ask the International Red Cross for help?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We did not make direct proposals like that to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree -- or, actually, I'll read out a portion of testimony from Stakic of the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D304, please. [In English] Before I continue, Your Honour, I forget to ask to tender 1D300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D300 becomes Exhibit D57, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 7749 of the Milomir Stakic trial transcript, lines 15 through 21. In line 15 you say: [In English] "We did not know really about the command structure." [Interpretation] Then in line 18, question: [In English] "And finally this: On this first afternoon, the soldiers who were there, were you able to understand from their uniforms who they were, what unit?" [Interpretation] Line 21, you say: [In English] "I wasn't able to tell really." [Interpretation] Can we agree that you were not familiar with the command structure in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: In the course of those first few days, we did not, because Major Kuruzovic arrived only several days later, and then we learned that he was the person in charge of camp. In the first few days, there was another officer. I don't remember his name, though, nor do I know what military unit he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which structure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, it would have been fair to the witness to have read to him also when he said something about the command structure, to read the question to him, which was limited at that first stage, not -- and that would have been appropriate to put to the witness because that was what his answer was about. Now the witness has corrected more or less, your mistake. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if I may just ask a question. I'm not quite sure that I'm following you now. At the time when you called for this exhibit, you had been asking the witness, did you communicate with members of the Red Cross. And then he said, we did communicate with -- no, no, no. You said did you suggest to them to ask the International Red Cross for help? And then it was said we did not make direct proposals like that to them. Next question was can we agree or actually I will read out a portion of testimony from Stakic on the 10th of September. That's when you called this. Now I thought what you -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not related. My mistake, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought what you wanted to show the witness is the fact that he asks the International Red Cross for help or somebody asked the International Red Cross for help.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this one of command structures I don't know when it comes from. When did you discuss command structures?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just moved to the next section of my questions, Your Honour, obviously I didn't [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... artfully enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that this exhibit is a basis for the command structure that's the topic you're now going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, Your Honour. Not Red Cross, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you made the transition clearer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will still dwell on the commands structure, doctor. Did you know at the time or do you know now what sort of organisation Kuruzovic belonged to? Who was his superior?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know who his superior was. I only know that he wore military camouflage uniform, and I don't know anything about his superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards the conditions in the camp, you described different guards and that you say that at some point or that there were periods of time when the guards only carried side-arms. Did you mean handguns?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. Just rifles without automatic rifles. Guards at Trnopolje changed. They rotated approximately every two weeks, and each shift had their own weapons, meaning that the kind of weapons changed with the guards. On one occasion, while I presume everyone was at the front line, we even had older men, retirees, with rifles who were tasked with guarding us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to the part of your statement where you discuss rape. It is paragraph 33. There, you mention Marica Olenjuk and a woman who came to her house. Can you recall that woman's name?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know her name, but I can show you the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I don't have a diagram let me ask you this: Is the house outside the perimeter at Trnopolje where the people were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was outside the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was a woman living in that house who came to see Marica Olenjuk; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You reported the incident to a skinny man in uniform; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: When I first came out, I saw Baltic in town, and he took me to that man, since he at that point in time was responsible for the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, the women were taken for medical examination?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that another incident?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was a different incident. The examinations took place later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was Rade Baltic -- Baltic's position? Why did you turn to him? Does he have a place in the Trnopolje hierarchy? Rade Baltic.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He was always in civilian clothes, much like Ostoja Skrbic. He did not wear a uniform. He was a prominent Serb in Trnopolje. Now whether he had any position, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said about Kuruzovic that he was in camouflage uniform. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was light olive-green camouflage fatigue. It was greenish in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see such uniform on other people at the time?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The Balaban brothers who came later had the same kind of uniform. As for Slavko Puhalic, his hue was different, darker.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to paragraph 63 of your statement. You will see it on the screen shortly. There, you say that you had a conversation with Dr. Ivic to have the women whom you reported as having been raped examined, and he consented to it. Ivic probably conveyed it to Kuruzovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few women who agreed to the report -- the incident being reported. I talked about it with Ivic, and he said that he needed to talk to some others first before a decision was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you present when he asked for Kuruzovic's approval, and do you know whether, indeed, he turned to Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I do know that he had to talk to someone first, although I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The women were taken to the hospital and examined; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They were put on a Serbian Red Cross van, and they were returned as well. Ivic confirmed to me that they had all been raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who told Ivic about that information?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Ivic accompanied them to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, the perpetrators, most likely, came to threatened Kuruzovic for having allowed that the women be examined; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They arrived two tanks. There were -- there were words El Manijakos on them. And they had an argument with Kuruzovic about why it was allowed for the women to be examined.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The letters on the tanks may have been El Manijakos as in mock Spanish. Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any impression that the perpetrators were trying to cover things up?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, very likely, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the first name of Dr. Ivic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dusko or Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, so that we could research that. One of the soldiers was detained once the women had been examined.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: We heard later on from the guards - I don't know whether it's true or not - that one of them was detained and that they went to get him out of jail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move on to that part of your statement where you discuss murders in Trnopolje. That section begins with paragraph 35. In paragraph 35, you say that they were taken away from the clinic and that they were no longer seen. The persons in question were Mijaz Gutic or Dzemal Zeric. Is it Zeric or Seric with a diacrytic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Zeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them being killed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, we only heard them being beaten and taken away in a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If they were killed you have no knowledge about who did that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, but they were taken away by people in military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who took them away in military uniform, you don't know who they were subordinated to, who they reported to?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but Slavko Puhalic knows because he called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need to go to paragraph 43 next. There you say -- well, you mentioned the brothers Pjanic and they told you of a murder of 20 people in the village of Elez. Who did they hear it from?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They said they heard it from the people who went to bury the bodies. It was organised by Pero Curguz to have them buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pero Curguz was a member of the Red Cross; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: He was. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who told you about it, who had heard about it from those who buried the bodies, those people didn't know who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: As in the case of other villages, that village was cleansed too, which means people were driven out of their homes and expelled, as well as killed there. Fikret Hodzic, he was killed in front of his house. There were soldiers in uniform. I don't know if it was the same unit that was engaged in mopping up everywhere, but that's how they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know if those people had been killed in combat and then brought there?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: They were not killed in combat, in Elez. That was right next to the camp. There was no fighting there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 55 of the statement, please. You discuss the killing of five people with the last name of Foric. Azra Blazevic told you about the killings; correct?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I saw when they were lined up, when they lined up the detainees in front of the school and they asked for Foric to step forward. Few of those lads stepped forward, and after that they were taken towards the railway, and we heard that they were killed. And Azra told me that she heard this from one of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who the guard is? Did she tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This person who told you Mrs. Blazevic, was that individual present during the killing or was that something that she also heard second-hand?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that I suppose she did not take part. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move now to paragraph 57. You speak about the killings at Ribnjak. Who told you about these killings?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That happened during the time when the International Red Cross was already on the site. A military vehicle brought some five or six young men into the camp. They were handed over to the guards. Mladen Mitrovic took them to the local commune building, and then another person in military uniform driving a civilian car arrived. Then they were beating these people for about half an hour and then took them towards Ribnjak, and while they were being taken away, we could see that they were being beaten along the way, and then we heard that they were killed down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, who told you that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's move on now to the topic of convoys from Trnopolje, although we did tackle this issue to a certain extent already. Were the people forced to enter buses or trains, or did they come to Trnopolje of their own accord?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. The people didn't come to Trnopolje of their own accord to board those vehicles. Once they were in Trnopolje, nobody beat them individually in order to force them to join the convoy. Quite simply, they were told to join the convoy along with the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the convoy was organised by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know who organised this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who organised the convoy with which you left?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: The International Red Cross and the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to Pero Curguz about who was organising the convoys?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pero Curguz was in charge, and he received instructions and orders from the Crisis Staff. That is what you told the federal criminal police.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, but I cannot say with any degree of certainty that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what we found on the 1st of December, 2004, page 19, that you said that. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot remember because I was in such a position that did not allow me to know 100 per cent who was giving orders whom among the Serbs. Of course, you don't think that the Serbs would come to me and tell me this and this order arrived from this and this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Would it be convenient time to make a break now because Mr. Mladic is not feeling well so maybe we could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can take a break now. Could you give us an indication as to how much time you would still need, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- I might finish today, or -- I -- I think I need a bit more time than we have until the end of the day, after the break. But I'll try my best to finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll consider how much time we would grant you. You know that we are always monitoring the cross-examination closely. We'll take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00. Could the witness first leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has closely monitored your cross-examination and expects you to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I realised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Preferably.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- myself as well, so I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, we don't have long. Let's now look at paragraphs 78 and 79 from your statement where you speak about the convoy headed for Mount Vlasic. Do you recall if this convoy set off on or around the 21st of August, 1992? Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It set off before the detainees were registered by the International Red Cross. So I think that the International Red Cross arrived at the camp but did not start registering them immediately. That means that the convoy was organised before they were registered. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't expecting you to give me an exact date. Now let me show you document 1D309. While we are waiting for this document to appear, this is issued by the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps, in which they are sending a report to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The date is the 22nd August 1992. However, there are two blank pages: Page 3 in B/C/S and page 2 in English. This is page 2. We need page 3 in B/C/S. Number 3, at the top of the page. Here, you can see when they describe the situation on the ground, it says, under number 3, fifth and sixth lines from the beginning: "On the 21st August between 1830 and 1900 hours, Muslim civilian men were massacred. The massacre was carried out by a group of policemen who were escorting the convoy towards Travnik. The place where the massacre took place was at Koricanske Stijene, in the canyon of Ilomska River on Mount Vlasic." Do you think that this is the incident that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. However, as I said, I cannot confirm the date positively, but I would think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next document is dated 11th September, and that's 1D311. The B/C/S version is quite poor whereas the English is a much better one, and I'm going to read out to you what it says. As I said, it's dated the 11th of September, 1992. It is addressed to the Banja Luka CSB, that is, the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka. And then it's passed on to the public security station in Prijedor. And it says: "I hereby order to conduct, in accordance with the law and other regulations ..." It seems to me that it says "a full investigation." "...regarding the fate of approximately 150 persons of Muslim nationality in the area of Skender Vakuf municipality - Koricanske Stijene." In order for me to put a question to you, we need to see another document, which is 1D310. It's a short document, dated 14th of September, 1992, in which the Prijedor public security station gives its response to the previous letter received from the Banja Luka CSB as their superiors. And we can see here that chief of public security station Prijedor reports to a higher authority that he was not able to carry out an investigation due to the fact that all police officers that were involved in escorting the convoy to Travnik, it says the 8th of 1992 [as interpreted], as of the 9th of September, 1992, were on the front line in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This is not correct. Because one of the Balaban brothers was there and the son of Pero Curguz who subsequently came to the camp and continued their regular work. They were not dispatched to the front. And the son of Curguz said himself that he did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Pero's son was a member of the police, because it is obvious from here that the police provided escort.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Pero's son was also dressed in a military drab olive uniform just like the Balaban brothers, but I don't know to which units he belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us today, if you know, that Dado Mrdza was convicted by this Tribunal for this crime as a member of the police force?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that for a simple reason that I recall these events only when I come here. Otherwise, I just close the book on it and never give it another thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina seven other persons were convicted in respect of this same event?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to tender 1D309.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What has this -- 1D309. Was the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's military document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D309 becomes Exhibit D58, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D58 is admitted into evidence. It is more or less from the bar table because the witness cannot tell us anything about it, isn't it, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He did tell us about the event. Who -- and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not about the document. Well -- no, I'm not saying it's not related. Of course, it is related to his evidence, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll use this document probably in a future, probably the Prosecution and us, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would also ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, by the way, Mr. Lukic, in the document we have on our screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says handwritten note, 15th of September, 1992. There is a handwritten note in the translation, which I cannot see on the original. So there apparently is something ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have those two documents, we found those two documents. Whether the Prosecution has different ones we have no objections to other documents that would be replaced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I notice is that the English version is not the same. And the way in which you sort that out with the Prosecution, I mean, most important is that it is sorted out, because translations should be in accordance with the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also ask to tender 1D310.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which is on the screen. So how to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Maybe we can inquire about whether we have the original in another way and whether this handwritten note is visible in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be marked for identification and so that we finally verify whether we have a good translation or an original with handwritten notes on it. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D310 becomes Exhibit D59, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, am I correct that you used 1D304 but you didn't not intend to tender it further or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1D -- I want to tender -- let me check, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, when we used transcripts usually we don't tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't tender them. You just have read it from the -- okay. That's then clear. And the same would be true then, I take it, for 1D311.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. 1D311 we would ask for [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would ask for that to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, for 1D311.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit D60, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D60 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next topic that I'd like to deal with you now, at the end, is the topic of dismissals from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 65 ter 17415.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you worked in the former system. We're of the same age. So we worked in Yugoslavia too. Do you know of the provisions of the law stating that whoever does not come to work for three days automatically loses his job. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I cannot say either yes or no, whether people are dismissed if they don't come to work for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. If we look at this list that is before us now, we see number 8 and number 9. Are these foreigners? These people had actually been dismissed. That is what is stated in the heading.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But, on the basis of their last names, can we not conclude that they're not from our part of the world?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether these are Albanian names from Kosovo. But I'm not aware of these people having worked in our institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Jelena Topic is number 11. Did you know her?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Jelena Topic would be a Serb?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Probably. I mean, I don't know how to make a distinction between Serb and Croat names, but if you say so, that's probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the name of Dr. Risto Stojanovski under 19.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He is most probably a Macedonian; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Twenty, Dr. Mario Karacic. Who could he be, or, rather, what could he be?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: A Croat, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grozdanic, Josipa?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Probably a Serb name. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 25, Jozica Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I think that is a Serb name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 50, Dusanka Vukovtic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Dusanka is a Serb name, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not to go on any further. That would it be roughly. Perhaps there are seven or eight other Serbs in this list. So I would like to ask you whether you heard at the time, or later, that all of those who did not report for work were dismissed from the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I know that those who reported to work were dismissed. I know that only those they needed were kept on, like Begic, the surgeon. They kept him in this hospital while they needed him. He's a traumatologist. When they no longer needed him they took him to Omarska and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When was Dr. Begic taken to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Kozarac. I cannot say exactly but he certainly worked for another month or so. When they found a replacement for him he was not released. He was taken to Omarska then. Begic. Then Sadikovic who took part in the negotiations they also took him to Omarska and killed him. Of course, he could not report for work if he was detained in a camp. I couldn't go to work either because I was detained in a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm saying. These people who worked in the General Hospital in Prijedor. If someone would not come to work for three days, three successive days, they automatically dismissed them?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Well, how could people go to work if they were detained in a camp by the Serbs themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But we cannot blame these people in the hospital for having dismissed these people if they did not come to work?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: But I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, this is not a debating club. You are supposed to ask questions and then the witness will answer those questions, as he did. And let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm close to the end. I would just --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know any of these people from this list? For example, did you --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Sadikovic Esad is number 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zoran Vikoli [phoen], you said you knew him?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. And also down here, a gynaecologist, Dr. Zeljko Sikora, he was taken to Omarska and killed. Of course, he was dismissed if he could not go to work. He was in camp and then he was killed there. And my wife was also dismissed. She could no longer go do work, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So do you know why these Serbs were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: For example Zoran Vikolo even before war started, managed to flee to Croatia, to Zagreb, and then he lost his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see that. It was the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I've already said there were many who were hiding and who did not want to fight against their neighbours. They were many such Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Major Kuruzovic was a teacher, actually; right?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He was just a reserve major. But otherwise before the war, he was a primary school teacher. I don't know what it was that he taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These were all the questions I had for you.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before I give an opportunity for the Prosecution to re-examine the witness. You asked the witness whether he could conclude with you, Mr. Lukic, that the names on the list that they are not from our part of the world. What is the common part of the world you have with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Balkans, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you say that these names are not from the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only two names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Only two names. Okay. Yes, it's just numbers 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I do have a few questions Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, first of all, I would like to go back to when you were asked today about a number of people wounded by the shellings during the attack in Kozarac. So I'm reading from temporary page number 40 of today's transcript and you said that, when asked you whether you could offer a figure, you said you come to the 6 to 7 and then later on you said, well, a total of 9. Now because I recall from your statement, and this is paragraph 12 to 18 to P269, that you described two different situations when you treated wounded people in Kozarac immediately at the beginning of the attack and later on in the following days. At the beginning of the attack, there was in the clinic of Kozarac, in the proper health centre and later on you moved to sort of house clinic, at the periphery Kozarac. So now I was wondering if could you clarify whether this number 9 that you told us about today, refers to the total number of wounded people, or just to the most serious cases that you mentioned while discussing -- while -- while replying to the answer by Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Just more serious cases. Those who came with minor injuries, I didn't take them into account.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's clear now. Later, yes. You also mentioned that the -- your wife's father, his wife, and his wife's sisters were killed in their house in Prijedor. Do you remember when was that? And do you know the circumstances in which that happened?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1994, considerably later. They didn't want to leave the house, and one night, there was this curfew in Prijedor that had been imposed. Men in uniform came and killed them in their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you know anything more about this uniform?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know exactly about that. But my wife and her brother investigated this for many years, and some of the persons who did that have already been brought before a court.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I've move to the next question. You also say today that some people came to the camp voluntarily -- yes, on their own accord. That they mostly came in an organised way by buses following the mopping up of their villages. I'm reading from temporary transcript of page 51 of today's transcript. Now, first of all, could you clarify the point in time in which this happened, meaning whether it was at the beginning when Trnopolje was established or later on after, before the journalists came?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: This of their own accord does not relate to these convoys with buses. These were individual cases, when some women came on their own, on foot, from the surrounding area, but these were just individual cases. All of those on buses and trucks were expelled from their homes and brought under duress.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. So just to clarify, the individual cases that you mentioned, did they represent as small percentage, I guess, of the camp population, could you maybe give an estimate in terms of numbers, like thousands or tens or less? I mean, just to give us a more precise idea.

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: It was a very small percentage. It was in such cases when they had been driven out of their homes by Serbs and told to go in the direction of Trnopolje. They were all in the area immediately surrounding Trnopolje. As for any specific figures, well, a few dozen, perhaps. It wasn't anywhere near the thousands of people that were included in convoys, but perhaps several dozen.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. Now, my next point, today you were asked by Mr. Lukic whether you knew to which organisation Kuruzovic belonged to, who was his superior. I'm now reading from temporary transcript page 63. And I just wanted to clarify your answer to that, because it seems to me that you just reply to the second part of the question. Who was his superior, and you say I don't know who his superior was. I only know that Kuruzovic wore a military camouflage uniform. And I don't know anything about his superiors. Can you -- well, my question was whether you knew to which -- exactly -- so whether you could give an answer to the first part of the question, meaning whether you knew to which organisation or which army, considering that you talk of a military camouflage uniform, Kuruzovic would be belong to or would be affiliated. If you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This, I would objection, Your Honour. Which army. There was only army. So it's not leading. It's more than leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: There is a military camouflage uniform mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know what -- wearing a camouflage uniform, do you know whether and to what armed force he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such uniforms were only worn by the military and the reserve force belonging to the military. There were no civilians. I can't be specific as to any unit though.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, finally, you were also asked the killings of five Muslim men with the last name Foric which you discuss at paragraph 55 of your statement. I just want to ask you whether in the months -- well, in the following months up until September, the end of September, 1992, you saw these five Muslim men with the last name Foric again in Trnopolje or not?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: No, no. The Forics were killed. I couldn't see them again. Later on, I only saw five survivors from Vlasic who came out at the same time we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Merdzanic.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Groome before we finish, I think we have one or two questions from the Bench still. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Merdzanic, could you tell us how many people approximately were employed by the Prijedor police -- by the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: There were all departments there such as internal medicine, surgery, gynaecology, so there were many people. As for the health centre where I worked there were fewer people. The health centre could have had about 100 employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the hospital --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: And the hospital must have had significantly more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means 500, 1.000, 2.000? What --

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Not as many. It wasn't a huge hospital, but several hundred people. I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Moloto has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At page 82, lines 10 to 13, you were explaining the individuals that you say were coming to the camp of their own accord and not the people in the buses. In explaining, you said these were people who came, for instance, after being "driven out of their homes by Serbs." Just quote that -- What I want to find out, the -- these people, are they, all of them, came there as a result of having been driven out of their homes by Serbs or are there others who came for other reasons, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Before the ICRC came, everyone who had come had to come there because they had been driven out of their homes and had nowhere else to go. Following the arrival of the ICRC, there were people who tried coming by themselves in order to be registered by the ICRC. Such registration offered a degree of safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So they were not coming to the camp to come in voluntarily to be in the camp. They were coming to be registered by the ICRC? Do I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So those who came, having been driven out of their homes by Serbs, what -- did they come to the camp or did they come to be registered also?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Those who had been thrown out had come before the ICRC came. They had nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I understand you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any questions triggered by the questions in re-examination or by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not by the Bench, by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, can we deal with it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question. Okay. Because I already have a bad reputation with -- with interpreters and other staff. So please. Further cross-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, it's me again. Is it correct that Kuruzovic had one type of uniform, Slavko Puhalic another, and the soldiers who were there, a third type?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: Slavko Puhalic and Major Kuruzovic had the same kind of uniform, a combat fatigue. It's just that Slavko Puhalic's was slightly darker. Most of the other soldiers had green military uniform, probably that of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time the army did not have combat fatigues?

utterances.speaker: IDRIZ MERDZANIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I just note that 65 ter number 17415 that was used by Mr. Lukic has not been tendered, and there is a reference on the record, of course names from that. So I was just wondering what the status is of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the list of some 119 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That one would show up again during this trial, I'm sure. So I asked for that document to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for that. Should we not mark it for identification at this moment because if at a later stage the same 65 ter number is beyond our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 17415.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit D61, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status until tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just for the record, we would have no objections to the document to be tendered now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Prosecution -- the Defence didn't do so, so, therefore, we leave it as it is now. Mr. Merdzanic, this concludes your evidence in this court. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With apologies to interpreters, technical staff, transcribers, everyone who is suffering under this late conclusion, we adjourn for the day, and we'll resume, Tuesday, the 2nd of October, at 9.30 in this same courtroom, I.
